notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 26, drawn from the sources I was able to access:

---

## Exodus 26 Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter describes the construction of the tabernacle itself (Hebrew *mishkān*, "dwelling"), a portable sanctuary that served Israel from Sinai until Solomon's temple. Ellicott notes the structure was 45 feet long by 15 feet wide, divided into the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place (Holy of Holies), set within a larger tent (*'ohel*) of goats' hair and further covered with rams' skins and an outer hide covering. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

David Guzik observes that the plans are revealed "from the inside out"—first the furniture (ch. 25), then the coverings and frame (ch. 26). "We approach the sanctuary from the outside in, but God builds the sanctuary from the inside out. He works in His people according to the same pattern." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

---

### v. 1 — The Ten Linen Curtains

**Traditional reading:** The "tabernacle" here (*mishkān*) refers to the inner tent proper. The ten curtains of fine twisted linen with blue, purple, and scarlet, with cherubim woven into them, formed the innermost layer, visible only from inside. Gill notes Jewish tradition (Maimonides, Jarchi) that the linen threads were six-fold or even twenty-four–fold twisted, producing a fabric of great substance. The cherubim were woven (not embroidered), so the design appeared on both sides. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

Gill further applies the linen mystically to the purity of Christ's human nature and the colours to the graces of the Spirit, or alternatively to Christ's wounds, bruises, and sufferings. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

Ellicott distinguishes between *ma'asêh khoshêb* (inwoven patterning, as here) and *ma'asêh rokêm* (needle embroidery, as in v. 36). Both techniques were well known in Egypt. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

The NET Bible notes that the coloured threads were likely used for embroidering the cherubim. — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Exo+26%3A1-2%2C7

Precept Austin adds that the tabernacle is the OT equivalent of Immanuel, "God with us" (Mt 1:23), ultimately fulfilled when Jesus Christ came to "tabernacle" among men (John 1:14). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-26-commentary

---

### v. 2 — Dimensions of Each Curtain

**Traditional reading:** Each curtain was 28 cubits long (about 42 feet / 14 metres) and 4 cubits wide (about 6 feet / 2 metres). Ellicott notes that Fergusson demonstrated a tent-cloth of almost exactly 28 cubits was needed to cover a space 20 cubits wide with sides meeting at a right angle. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 3–4 — Joining the Curtains and Blue Loops

**Traditional reading:** Five curtains were sewn together to form one large piece, and the other five to form another. The purpose of making two sets rather than one was portability—the entire covering would have been too heavy to carry in one piece. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

Loops of blue material were placed on the edge ("selvedge") of each set at the point where they were to be coupled. Gill notes the loops were not woven in but made afterwards, probably with a needle. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 5–6 — Fifty Loops and Gold Clasps

**Traditional reading:** Fifty loops on each curtain edge, corresponding one to another, joined by fifty gold clasps ("taches"). These were likely split-rings or links like modern sleeve-links. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

Guzik sees a spiritual principle: "unity in diversity." The two separate sets become "one tabernacle," illustrating Romans 12:5—"we, being many, are one body in Christ." Trapp (cited by Guzik) suggests it further pictures the Church in heaven and earth as one. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

---

### v. 7 — The Goats' Hair Covering

**Traditional reading:** The second layer was curtains of goats' hair—a dark, coarse, weather-resistant material (like modern felt) still used by Bedouins for tent-making. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/ and https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-26-commentary

There were eleven curtains (one more than the linen set), because one served at the entrance where there was no linen curtain. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

Gill sees the goats' hair as typifying Christ's outward appearance: attended with human infirmities, in the form of a servant, in meanness and poverty, yet "all rich and glorious within." — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 8–9 — Dimensions and Coupling of Goats' Hair Curtains

**Traditional reading:** Each goats' hair curtain was 30 cubits (45 feet) long and 4 cubits wide—two cubits longer than the linen curtains, so they hung lower on the sides for better weather protection. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

The eleven were divided into five sewn together and six sewn together. The sixth curtain was doubled over at the front (east end) of the tent, giving "a sort of finish to the roof in the front of the structure" (Ellicott) and described by Jarchi (cited by Gill) as "like a modest bride that covers her face with a veil." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm and https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 10–11 — Bronze Clasps

**Traditional reading:** Unlike the gold clasps of the inner linen layer, the goats' hair curtains were joined by fifty bronze clasps. Gill notes the coarser material and loops received clasps of a "meaner metal," yet they joined the tent together just as effectively. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 12–13 — The Overlap

**Traditional reading:** The goats' hair covering was wider and longer than the linen one. The extra half-curtain hung down at the back (west end), and an extra cubit hung over each side (north and south). Thus the beautiful linen layer was completely obscured—"Heaven remained hidden to all except those who entered in through the door of the tabernacle." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

---

### v. 14 — Ram Skins Dyed Red and Fine Leather

**Traditional reading:** Two outer coverings: (1) ram skins dyed red (like fine morocco leather with the wool removed), and (2) an outer covering of "badger skins" (KJV) or possibly "porpoise/sea-cow skins"—a durable, water-resistant hide. No dimensions are given for these coverings. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

Ellicott reasons their purpose was to keep out rain, so they must have covered at minimum the roof ridge and likely the whole *mishkān*. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

Gill comments that the four layers (linen, goats' hair, rams' skins, badgers' skins) show the care God takes of His church: "clothed with Christ's righteousness, and under the purple covering of his blood, and surrounded by his almighty power" (cf. Isaiah 4:5). — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

The NET Bible summarizes the movement from inside to outside: the pure linen represented God's righteousness, the goats' hair was a reminder of sin (through the daily sin offering of a goat), the rams' skins dyed red recalled sacrifice and priestly ministry set apart by blood, and the outer covering marked separation between God and the world. — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Exo+26%3A1-2%2C7

---

### vv. 15–16 — The Boards (Frames)

**Traditional reading:** The wooden framework was made of acacia wood boards standing upright. Each board was 10 cubits (15 feet / 5 metres) high and 1.5 cubits (2 feet 3 inches) wide. They were overlaid with gold (v. 29). There is scholarly debate about whether the boards formed a solid wall or an open frame; Guzik thinks a solid wall is more likely. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

Gill says these boards denote "such who are pillars in the house of God" and "the church itself is the pillar and ground of truth" (Galatians 2:9). — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

---

### v. 17 — Two Tenons per Board

**Traditional reading:** Each board had two projections (tenons, literally "two hands" in Hebrew) at its lower end, shaped to fit into mortises in the silver sockets. They were "set in order one against another"—spaced at regular intervals to correspond to their sockets. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm and https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 18–21 — Twenty Boards on South and North Sides

**Traditional reading:** Twenty boards each for the south and north sides, with forty silver sockets under each side (two per board, one per tenon). Since each board was 1.5 cubits wide, 20 boards × 1.5 cubits = 30 cubits (45 feet) for the length of the tabernacle. The tabernacle faced east, so south was on the right. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

---

### v. 19 — Forty Silver Bases

**Traditional reading:** Each silver socket (base) weighed one talent of silver (about 264 pounds / 120 kg). Guzik sees silver as "the metal of redemption" (cf. Exodus 21:32; Leviticus 5:15; Matthew 26:15). Thus the entire tabernacle rested on a foundation of redemption, pointing to Christ's redeeming work. Furthermore, the silver separated the tabernacle from the dirt of the desert floor—"Jesus' redeeming work separates us from the world." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

Gill calculates each talent of silver at about 353 pounds weight (using Bishop Cumberland's estimate), noting the hundred sockets (total) correspond to the hundred talents of silver collected at the numbering of the people (Exodus 38:25). — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 22–25 — The West (Rear) Side and Corner Boards

**Traditional reading:** Six boards for the west (rear) side, plus two corner boards. The corner boards coupled the sides to the back, being joined at both top and bottom by a single ring. This made eight boards total for the rear, with sixteen silver sockets. The total width came to about 10 cubits (15 feet). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

Gill cites Lightfoot's detailed reconstruction: the corner planks joined end and side together, with a quarter-cubit inward making up the breadth, a quarter taken by the thickness of the adjoining side plank, and a quarter outward. Lightfoot adds that these corners "knit end and side together, and were the strength of the building; as Christ is of his church, making Jews and Gentiles one spiritual temple." — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 26–28 — The Crossbars

**Traditional reading:** Five crossbars per side (south, north, and west), made of acacia wood and overlaid with gold. Four bars ran on the outside of each wall, while the central (middle) bar ran through the midst of the boards from end to end—invisible from the outside.

Guzik sees this middle bar as speaking of "both the visible and invisible unity among God's people." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

Ellicott adds that the bars were passed through gold rings attached to the boards, each board having at least one such ring, and they were "probably placed outside the tabernacle walls." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

---

### v. 29 — Gold Overlay

**Traditional reading:** The boards themselves were overlaid with gold, gold rings were attached to hold the crossbars, and the crossbars were also overlaid with gold. The interior of the tabernacle was thus a golden enclosure, fit for the presence of God.

---

### v. 30 — According to the Pattern

**Traditional reading:** God repeats the command to build "according to the pattern shown you on the mountain" (cf. Exodus 25:9, 25:40). This indicates Moses received a vision—a visual revelation—of exactly how the tabernacle should look, which he then had to communicate to the craftsmen. Guzik applies this to leadership: "God works the same way in leaders today. He gives them a vision of what His work should be, and the leader passes it on to others." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

The Precept Austin commentary cites Hebrews 8:5; 9:23–24; 10:1 to show that the tabernacle was "a copy and shadow of heavenly things," not the ultimate reality. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-26-commentary

---

### vv. 31–33 — The Veil

**Traditional reading:** The veil was made of the same materials as the inner linen curtain—blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, with cherubim woven in. It hung on four pillars of acacia wood overlaid with gold, standing on four silver sockets, and was suspended by gold hooks.

Ellicott notes that the veil was "of the essence of the *mishkān*"—it had to have an outer and an inner sanctuary. The high priest alone could enter behind the veil, and only once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2–34; Hebrews 9:7). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

Guzik provides the key New Testament application: "In the temple, this veil was torn from top to bottom at the death of Jesus (Matthew 27:51), showing that through His death, there is no longer a barrier to the Most Holy place." Hebrews 10:19–20 teaches that we now enter "through the veil, that is His flesh." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

F. B. Meyer (cited by Guzik) laments: "How many there are who never get beyond the dividing vail! They know the brazen altar of Atonement, the laver of daily washing, the golden altar of intercession; but they are never admitted to that blessed intimacy of communion which sees the Shechinah glory." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

Ellicott notes it is uncertain whether "under the taches" (the clasps joining the two halves of the linen covering) means the Holy of Holies was directly under them—if so, the two chambers would be equal in size; if not, the Holy of Holies was likely half the size of the Holy Place (as in Solomon's temple). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

---

### vv. 34–35 — Arrangement of Furniture

**Traditional reading:** The Ark of the Testimony (with the mercy seat) was placed behind the veil in the Most Holy Place. Outside the veil, the table of showbread was on the north side (right as one entered from the east), and the lampstand on the south side (left). The altar of incense, though not mentioned in this chapter, stood between them closer to the veil (Exodus 30:6; 40:26). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

Guzik notes the furniture in the holy place spoke of three great obligations: prayer (altar of incense), fellowship (table of showbread), and illumination (lampstand). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

---

### vv. 36–37 — The Screen (Door) for the Entrance

**Traditional reading:** The entrance screen on the east side was made of the same coloured materials (blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen) but was "embroidered" (*ma'asêh rokêm*) rather than woven with in-patterned cherubim as the inner curtain and veil were. It hung from gold hooks on five pillars of acacia wood overlaid with gold, set in five bronze sockets. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

Ellicott observes that the odd number of five pillars (compared to four for the inner veil) is "surprising" until one remembers that a tent of this shape requires a central tent-pole in the gable-end with equal supports on either side—this central pillar, together with the use of the word *'ohel*, gives "the tent theory of Mr. Fergusson, now generally adopted, its solid basis." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/26.htm

Guzik notes that bronze, refined by fire, "pictures purity and endurance through trial." The entrance to the tabernacle hung on a symbolic foundation of bronze—what Jesus did for us. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

---

## Traditions and Differing Emphases

### Typological / Christological Reading (Broadly Protestant Evangelical)

This is the most common approach across Evangelical, Reformed, Baptist, and Pentecostal sources examined. Gill (Baptist/Calvinistic) reads the tabernacle as a type of Christ's human nature ("the true tabernacle which God pitched," Hebrews 8:2). The fine linen signifies His purity; the coloured threads represent the graces of the Spirit or His sufferings; the cherubim represent the ministration of angels to Him. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/26.htm

Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic) likewise reads the tabernacle Christologically but emphasizes application to the believer's inner life: God builds "from the inside out." The silver foundation points to redemption; the veil torn at Christ's death opens access to intimacy with God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/

### Catholic Reading

The Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent) describes the tabernacle as the "dwelling-tent of God" and notes the same structural details, emphasizing that "the wooden framework, though indispensable, being only of secondary importance"—the curtains were primary because it was essentially a tent. The dimensions given match the traditional account. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14424b.htm (searched excerpt)

Haydock's Catholic Commentary (Challoner's notes) adds that the veil was "the other veil, which was rent at the death of Christ" and cites Baronius that "Christian temples were formerly built in imitation of the Jewish tabernacle. It was a figure of the Catholic church" (1 Timothy 3:15). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/exodus-26.html

The Douay-Rheims (Challoner) text calls the mercy seat "the propitiatory" and the Most Holy Place "the holy of holies (literally, the sanctuaries of the sanctuary), as being the most holy of all holy places." — https://ccel.org/ccel/challoner/douayrheims/Exodus/26.html

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible / Expositor's Bible Commentary)

The NET Bible notes emphasize that the passage can be studied on two levels: (1) its practical and symbolic function for Israel's worship, and (2) its typology, where "the tabernacle and many of its parts speak of Christ." — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Exo+26%3A1-2%2C7

The Expositor's Bible Commentary (via StudyLight) addresses structural confusion about the temple/tabernacle terminology and credits Mr. Fergusson's tent theory (published in Smith's Bible Dictionary, "Temple") with "solving all the problems connected with the measurements of the tabernacle, and bringing order into what was little more than chaos before." The key insight is that the tabernacle was "a real tent with sloping sides, not a flat cover laid upon the flat inner structure of boards." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-26.html

### On Images in Worship

John Trapp (cited by both Guzik and Precept Austin) makes an anti-image argument: the cherubim were "Golden-winged images, made by God's special appointment, and set out of sight. Hence then is no warrant for the use of images in churches." This reflects a Reformed/Puritan polemic against religious imagery. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-26/ and https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-26-commentary

---

**Note on limitations:** Due to search constraints, I was unable to access specific verse-by-verse material from Lutheran sources (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan sources (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), or Orthodox sources (oca.org) distinct from the Catholic material above. The Reformed and Baptist views accessed (Gill, Guzik, the sources at Precept Austin) represent a broad Evangelical typological consensus rather than sharply differing denominational positions on this chapter.
